source.version: Undated manuscript PDF on file. No manuscript date, arXiv version identifier, or journal publication citation is printed on the title page (p. 1). The exact version is not confirmed by this document; the candidate record is not used as version evidence.
source.title_on_document: Epitome: Pioneering an Experimental Platform for AI-Social Science Integration

supplement.where: Separate Supplementary Information is cited on pp. 10, 12 and 18. The data-availability statement links https://github.com/epitome-AISS/epitome for further information, without a direct supplementary-file link (p. 18). A Nature Research Reporting Summary is mentioned on p. 16, which contains no actionable link. The saved PDF ends with references on p. 25 and has no embedded supplementary files.
supplement.holds: The paper says detailed case-study data and experimental materials are in Supplementary Information (p. 18). It cites Supplementary Figure 10 for writing output quality, Figures 9 and 11-13 for completion time and participant-reported outcomes (p. 10), Figures 21-22 for creativity results, Tables 2-3 and Figure 33 for moral-reasoning results (p. 12), and Section G for the platform manual (p. 18). These materials are absent from the supplied PDF; their participant counts, arm statistics and standard errors cannot be verified.

paper_design_summary: The platform paper reports three case studies: managers assigned to ChatGPT or Overleaf for incentivized writing, story writers randomly assigned zero, one or five AI ideas, and moral-reasoning simulations involving AI agents and human participants (pp. 9-13). Experts scored writing quality, content quality and originality in the writing studies; the text also reports summary output quality, individual creativity and collective diversity (pp. 9-12). The professional-writing study analyzed 35 people, while the story-writing participant count is unstated and its figure labels 31 stories (p. 9, Fig. 2; p. 11, Fig. 3a).

studies.label: Case Study 1: professional writing (Noy and Zhang replication)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Managers were allocated to ChatGPT versus Overleaf through the Random Design module (p. 10). Fig. 2a shows a common Task 1 before tool sign-up and a Task 2 after sign-up; the caption describes two incentivized tasks and training on the respective tools (p. 9). Between-person tool assignment is combined with repeated writing tasks; the main text does not specify the statistical model for this structure.

task.description: Two incentivized writing tasks for managers, evaluated through expert blind review of writing quality, content quality and originality. The exact task prompts are not specified in the main text (p. 9, Fig. 2a and caption). Originality is an output criterion, supporting inclusion of the writing outcomes in this screening.

studies.label: Case Study 2: adventure stories, English and Chinese conditions (Doshi and Hauser replication)

The single contrast below preserves the joint narrative; it is not a computed pooled contrast and does not allocate the reported range or tests to particular AI arms or languages.

studies.label: Case Study 3: Heinz Dilemma and human-AI courtroom simulations

assignment.what_was_assigned: The authors configured AI characters for a town simulation, then used these agents in courtroom simulations with human participants (pp. 12-13). Random assignment of people to AI assistance versus another condition is not reported. These are phases of one reported case study, not documented randomized assistance arms.

assignment.locator: p. 12, Moral reasoning in human-AI interactions; p. 13, Fig. 4 caption.

participants.exclusions: Not stated. The seven characters in the first phase are AI agents, not people (pp. 12-13). No human sample size is given, and the moral-reasoning test degrees of freedom are not converted into a participant count.
participants.who: Human participants interacted with AI agents in courtroom roles such as judges, jurors and witnesses; recruitment and demographics are not stated (p. 13, Fig. 4 caption).

task.description: Moral reasoning about Heinz stealing medicine for his wife, first in an AI town and then in a courtroom with human participants. eligibility.reason: Case Study 2 randomly assigns people to Human-only, one AI-generated suggestion or five AI-generated suggestions for adventure-story writing, and experts score the produced stories for writing quality, content quality and originality (p. 11, Fig. 3 caption). Criteria 1 and 3 are met. The number of distinct people analyzed is not stated; neither the 31 stories in Fig. 3a nor the test degrees of freedom on p. 12 establish that at least 50 people were analyzed in this study. Criterion 2 and core eligibility remain unclear. Case Study 1 analyzed 35 people after exclusions and independently fails the sample-size threshold (p. 9, Fig. 2 caption). Case Study 3 has no qualifying creativity or diversity outcome (pp. 12-14, Moral reasoning in human-AI interactions and Fig. 4). Counts cannot be combined across these studies or inferred from stories, ratings or AI agents. The separately cited Supplementary Information, absent from the saved PDF, is needed to verify Case Study 2 sample flow and distinct analyzed people across arms and languages (p. 18).

one_line_finding: The story-writing replication reports individual-creativity increases of 42.1% with one AI idea and 16.4% with five, alongside a 5.64%-6.47% decline in collective diversity, but does not state the analyzed participant count (p. 12; p. 11, Fig. 3).
open_questions: How many people were randomized and analyzed in each story-writing arm and language, what exclusions occurred, and what does the 31-story corpus in Fig. 3a cover?
What are the statistical observation units and rating-aggregation rules for the writing-quality, content-quality and originality dimensions in both writing studies?
How many observations underlie the headline individual-creativity results, and how do they relate to the 31 stories in Fig. 3a?
How are the headline output-quality and individual-creativity scores defined, and how do they relate to the three named expert-rated dimensions?

What is the collective-diversity metric, which outputs are compared, and which AI arm or language corresponds to each percentage and t statistic? Which tests have p < 0.05 and df = 28, and how was dependence handled?
Can the cited Supplementary Information and Reporting Summary provide the missing sample counts, arm-level statistics, scoring scales and analysis specifications?
What exact manuscript version and deployed model configurations correspond to this saved PDF? Fig. 3c confirms only the illustrated gpt-4 workflow labels.
Do the English and Chinese conditions use separate samples, and is there overlap between any case studies?
For Case Study 1, what were the randomized and analyzed arm sizes and exclusion timing, and how do Task 1 and Task 2 enter the reported quality analysis?
For Case Study 3, was any human assignment performed, what was its unit, and how many people were analyzed? This case has no qualifying creativity outcome.
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09 from both valid raw forms and the source. The complete markdown conversion was read in four consecutive chunks, through all references. Figures 2 and 3 were rendered in memory and visually checked, including 35 Managers, 31 stories and the gpt-4 labels. No external version or unverified candidate lead supplied an extraction value. Locators are one-based PDF page positions. Both screeners listed the same outcome inventory; S2 outcome order differed, so outcomes were matched by name and the final IDs follow B. Differences count model identification once, six analysis-unit fields, six per-dimension contrast arrays, one summary-outcome observation count, and the Case Study 3 assignment unit. Wording, arm-name aliases, missing values expressed as empty strings versus null, outcome ordering, and equivalent locators were not counted as differences. Each reconciliation resolved object gives the final value and its reason. n_unresolved counts unresolved difference entries; additional unknown facts agreed by both screeners, especially the Case Study 2 participant count, appear in agreed_fields_checked with confirmed=false and in open_questions. No separate dimension-specific contrast is recorded when the paper only names the scored dimension. The headline scores and named rating dimensions are retained separately because their relationship is undefined; they are not established independent effects. All analytical units that the source does not specify remain null. Fig. 3a labels a single corpus of 31 stories. The final form retains this count only in descriptive prose; n_units is null for all S2 outcomes because the figure does not establish their analysis observation counts. The label does not establish 31 participants or three independent samples. The source does not explain its relationship to the headline tests. The diversity statistics remain a joint narrative with no inferred allocation to arms or languages and no computed pooling. The printed t = 54.80 is retained. Case Studies 1 and 2 are coded online_rct for their Epitome web/survey implementation (pp. 7, 9-11 and 16); recruitment panels and physical testing locations are not specified. Between-person tool assignment and repeated tasks support the mixed structure in Case Study 1 (p. 9, Fig. 2a). English and Chinese story conditions remain in one study because separate participant samples are not established. AI availability and immediate timing describe production of the assisted work, not subsequent expert evaluation. No unassisted creative output after AI removal is reported. The source does not designate a primary outcome or report a preregistration. Completion time and self-reported attitudes, efficacy and enjoyment are outside the output-based creativity questions. The moral study is retained for completeness with no qualifying outcome. No participant counts were inferred from degrees of freedom or outputs, and no effects were calculated. No form was missing or unparsable. Finalized on 2026-10-09 after reading all 322 lines of the markdown conversion through the final reference; there is no appended supplement. The 25-page PDF, its zero embedded files, the relevant page text and the figure labels on pp. 9 and 11 were independently checked with PyMuPDF; figures were rendered in memory without creating files. The three outcome-lens problems are corrected, the people-lens sample-size gap remains open, and the assignment challenge contains no problems. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as a historical record; its instruction to retain 31 in the named dimension outcome counts is superseded by the final challenge resolutions. Case Studies 1 and 2 are reported replications, with no stated reuse of original participants, so their randomized design coding is retained. Each open question and all eight unresolved reconciliation differences are addressed in final.open_items, combining overlapping questions and the six analysis-unit differences. open_items.item: Case Study 2 randomized and analyzed people by arm and language, exclusions, and coverage of the 31-story corpus (open question 1). The missing Supplementary Information/Reporting Summary sought in open question 6 must establish the distinct analyzed-person count for criterion 2; arm statistics, scales and analysis specifications are also missing. Sources: pp. 10-12, Fig. 3; p. 16, Reporting summary; p. 18, data availability.

Statistical observation units and rating aggregation for Writing quality, Content quality and Originality in S1 and S2 (open question 2 and all six unresolved reconciliation outcomes[].unit differences). An analysis specification is needed for extraction, but criterion 3 is already met by explicit expert scoring of produced work (p. 9, Fig. 2 caption; p. 11, Fig. 3 caption).

Observation counts for S2 headline individual-creativity tests and their relationship to the 31 stories (open question 3 and unresolved reconciliation studies[S2].outcomes[Individual creativity].n_units). The test sample and rating aggregation remain unknown (pp. 11-12); they do not substitute for the distinct-person count addressed separately under criterion 2.

Definitions, scales and aggregation of the headline output-quality and individual-creativity scores, including their relationship to the three expert-rated dimensions (open question 4; pp. 9-12). Needed to prevent duplicate or misclassified estimates; output-scored originality already establishes criterion 3.

Collective-diversity metric, compared outputs, arm/language mapping of percentages and tests, scope of p < 0.05 and df = 28, and dependence handling (open question 5; p. 12, Human creativity and generative AI). Needed for diversity-effect extraction and precision assessment; criterion 3 is independently supported by expert-rated originality.

Exact version of the saved undated manuscript and deployed model configurations by arm/language (open question 7). Author identification of the saved document and actual deployment is needed; Fig. 3c only confirms the illustrated gpt-4 labels. These details do not change the documented random assignment to generative-AI assistance or output scoring.

Whether English and Chinese conditions contain distinct or overlapping participants, and whether participants overlap among case studies (open question 8; pp. 10-12). Language-sample overlap affects the unique-person total for S2 and hence criterion 2; overlap across case studies affects sample identification, and separate studies cannot be added to pass the threshold.

S1 randomized/analyzed arm sizes, exclusion timing, and how Task 1 and Task 2 enter the quality analysis (open question 9; pp. 9-10, Fig. 2). Needed for extraction, but the verified total of 35 people analyzed already falls below the core threshold.

S3 human assignment procedure, assignment unit and analyzed-person count (open question 10 and unresolved reconciliation studies[S3].assignment.unit). These remain unstated, but no further information is needed to decide this case study: the reported outcomes concern moral reasoning, sentiment and verdicts, without a qualifying creativity or diversity outcome (pp. 12-14, Fig. 4).
